items.author: secretsofuniverse
items.text:
🐋 Whale calls have revealed a strange echo of Einstein’s relativity.

Scientists studying how whale sounds travel underwater have found an unexpected wave effect that can make sound appear to outrun its normal speed limit.

Whales are often tracked using hydrophones, underwater microphones that compare when a call reaches different receivers.

But if a whale is close to the ocean surface, its call does not take just one path.

Some sound travels directly to the receiver. Some bounces off the surface first.

When those two paths meet, they can interfere with each other and shift the strongest peak of the signal earlier than expected.

That can make the wave packet seem to move faster than sound in seawater, which is usually about 1,500 meters per second.

In simulations, some apparent speeds reached around 3,000 meters per second.

But this does not break physics.

The information carried by the wave still stays within the true speed limit. Only the peak of the combined signal appears to jump ahead.

That is the Einstein connection.

Special relativity allows wave shapes to behave strangely, but it does not allow information to outrun light.

A whale call may have exposed a subtle trick of waves, and it could make future whale tracking far more accurate.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Spiesberger et al., “Supersonic and superluminal energy and speed of information via temporal interference in a dispersionless environment”, Physical Review E (2026)

items.text:
Hitting the afternoon slump? Well, you're in luck; let's talk about the weather headlines for the rest of the week! There's no doubt today is gorgeous, so try to find time outside later! 

Wednesday: High pressure will start moving back in and taking back control of our weather, so it will warm up a little more and get a bit more humid across the state, but it should still be another really nice day overall! 

Thursday & Friday: Heat and humidity will really crack back up, so it'll be hot and humid with highs in the upper 80s and low/mid 90s for most areas outside of the higher elevations of the mountains. As a moist flow starts to move back in, the risk of scattered showers and thunderstorms will increase. Very isolated chance Thursday, but Friday looks higher, with some isolated to scattered storms around mainly in the afternoon and evening. 

The North Carolina Weekend: Hard to believe, but the weekend is just around the corner. We will see a front around, so there will be scattered showers and thunderstorms throughout the day, but especially in the afternoon and evening. No washouts, but some storms will definitely be around; we can't rule out a strong-to-severe storm chance, mainly with gusty to damaging winds. Will keep you posted! Highs are generally in the 80s to the low 90s for the weekend. 

-Ethan

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
RECORD-SETTING QUIET HURRICANE SEASON...SO FAR

The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season has been remarkably quiet, with just five named storms and still no hurricanes. The well-advertised, historic El Niño has certainly helped put the brakes on tropical activity.

Just how quiet has it been? Through September 8, this season has produced the lowest Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) of any Atlantic season since 1950.

ACE measures how active a hurricane season is by factoring in both storm strength and how long storms last. The stronger and longer-lived the storms, the higher the ACE.

This year’s ACE through September 8 is a measly 4.4. For some perspective, in 1995 it had already reached a whopping 148.5 by this same point!

And another record may be just around the corner. It’s looking increasingly likely we’ll make it past September 11 without a hurricane, which would make 2026 the latest on record for the Atlantic’s first hurricane.

There’s still plenty of hurricane season left, of course, but with all the weather hype and doom-and-gloom these days, it’s nice to talk about a good weather record for a change!

REFRESHER TIME! 🌪 TORNADO WATCH vs TORNADO WARNING!

I got yelled at quite a bit by people for my Hawaii post about their first tornado watch, saying I was wrong because Hawaii has had tornado warnings before. While yes, Hawaii has had tornado warnings before, they've never had a watch before. There is a difference!

🔴WATCH: Conditions are favorable for tornadoes. Storms may or may not have even formed yet. This is the time to be aware that things could get serious later on. Have a way to receive the latest information, and know what you're going to do.

🔴WARNING: A tornado has been detected by radar, or spotted by a chaser/EMS/spotter. Seek shelter!

The same applies for severe thunderstorms as well!

Iowa could be seeing severe weather today...

Daytime heating and very moist dew points will generate moderate to strong instability, with convergence along an advancing cold front triggering a gradual increase in thunderstorm coverage from mid to late afternoon. With deep-layer shear vectors oriented parallel to the front, initial storms are expected to rapidly grow upscale into organized line segments.

Severe wind gusts will be the primary hazard as these outflow-dominant storms track through the region into the evening. Poor mid-level lapse rates will limit the large hail threat, while a localized increase in low-level shear over central Iowa may support a brief tornado.

Hurricane Lowell is bringing heavy rain, strong winds and even a tornado threat to Hawaii’s western islands.

It’s the second hurricane to impact Hawaii this season, following Hurricane Lala in mid-August.

Meanwhile, here in the Atlantic, we still haven’t had our first hurricane of the season, and I’m perfectly fine keeping it that way! 

You may have noticed that both hurricanes to impact Hawaii start with the letter “L”. The two “L” storms are just a coincidence. Lala formed in the Central Pacific, where storms use a separate, continuous list of Hawaiian names that doesn’t restart each year. Lowell formed in the Eastern Pacific, where storms use the traditional alphabetical naming system. Two different basins, two different naming systems, both just happened to give us an “L” storm.
🌀🌀

items.text:
MID-MONTH MOISTURE SIGNAL FOR THE SOUTHWEST & SOUTHERN PLAINS🌵🌧️⛈️there continues to be an encouraging signal for increased moisture and precipitation across a large part of the Southwest and eventually the Southern Plains heading into mid-September!

The latest 6-10 day outlook for September 13-17 favors above-normal precipitation across Arizona, New Mexico, Utah, Colorado and much of the Great Plains, including West Texas, North Texas and Oklahoma. This is due to a persistent trough near the West Coast combined with the broader upper-level pattern should favor increased precipitation from the Southwest through the Rockies and into much of the Plains.

The wetter signal continues in the 8-14 day period, September 15-21. Above-normal precipitation is favored across much of the West, while Oklahoma and essentially all of Texas are also favored to see above-normal precipitation. Kansas and Nebraska remain on the wetter side of the outlook as well.

For the Southwest, the pattern could become particularly active. Southerly flow may help transport deeper moisture northward, with the potential for a surge of Gulf of California moisture. There is currently a risk for heavy precipitation across parts of the Desert Southwest and Great Basin from September 15-19, along with a risk of flooding.

While it won't rain every day or everywhere, the broader trend is for increasing moisture and more opportunities for precipitation from the Southwest into parts of the Southern Plains during the middle and latter part of September🌵🌧️⛈️

ANOTHER EARLY-SEASON STORM SYSTEM COULD BRING WEATHER CHANGES TO THE NORTHWEST THIS WEEKEND BUT THERE ARE QUESTION🌧️❄️💨⛈️ confidence continues to increase that an upper-level trough will drop south out of British Columbia late Friday into the weekend, bringing the potential for a fall-like pattern change to parts of the Pacific and Inland Northwest, and eventually the Northern U.S. Rockies.

There are questions on how widespread rain will be but showers should become increasingly likely across Washington and into northern Oregon and Idaho. The best opportunity for a wetter period currently favors Washington and northern Idaho, while precipitation could become more limited farther south but it depends on how deep the storm system becomes and how far north or south it tracks. A few thunderstorms may accompany the system across parts of northeast Washington and northern Idaho as colder air aloft moves overhead.

The trough will send much cooler air south across the Northwest, with the cooling eventually reaching northern California and the Sierra. This comes after a significant midweek warm-up, so the change could be especially noticeable. Breezy to locally gusty winds are also expected as the system moves through.

Colder air could should lower snow levels down to 6,000-7,000 feet in Washington and Oregon and 7,000-8,000 feet across parts of Idaho and the Northern U.S. Rockies, allowing some of the highest peaks to pick up accumulating snow. It's uncertain how much snow Washington and Oregon see but there's higher confidence in snow from Idaho into Montana and Wyoming.

There is still high uncertainty regarding exactly how deep and far south this system digs. A deeper-slower storm would support more widespread rain, colder temperatures and greater mountain snow potential. A farther north or east track would keep precipitation more limited, particularly across Oregon and northern California🌧️❄️💨⛈️

APPETIZER COLD FRONT THIS WEEK | BIGGER FRONT NEXT WEEK🌧️⛈️📉changes are increasingly likely beginning late this Wednesday into Thursday.

A cold front is forecast to drop south out of Kansas Wednesday night as the strong ridge responsible for the heat begins to break down. Showers and thunderstorms should develop along and ahead of the front and spread south into Oklahoma Wednesday night and Thursday. Rain chances have notably increased across northern Oklahoma, where some areas now have a decent shot at seeing much-needed rain, favoring locations north of I-40 late Wednesday, and it now appears the front will make it down to near the Red River late Thursday.

While this won't be a strong fall cold front, it should finally weaken the persistent heat ridge, bring at least some temperature relief and provide the best opportunity for more widespread rain that parts of Oklahoma have seen recently, and should drop temperatures into the upper 80s in far northern Oklahoma with highs in the low 90s down to I-40 - instead of 100-105 - and knock lows into the lower 60s - maybe some upper 50s for far northern Oklahoma. A stronger front moves in next week with a bigger temperature drop🌧️⛈️📉

HAWAII HURRICANE WARNING‼️🚨🌀a Hurricane Warning is now in effect for Kauaʻi and Niʻihau as Hurricane Lowell’s forecast track has shifted east, bringing the powerful storm closer to the western Hawaiian Islands! A Tropical Storm Watch is also in effect for Oʻahu.

Lowell remains a Category 3 hurricane with sustained winds of 115 mph, moving north-northeast at 14 mph. The center is forecast to pass just west of Kauaʻi County late today into early Tuesday, but even a small additional shift east or west could significantly change the impacts. Hurricane-force winds are now possible on Kauaʻi and Niʻihau, with tropical-storm-force winds potentially reaching Oʻahu.

Heavy rain and thunderstorms will affect the entire state through Tuesday and could linger into Wednesday. The Honolulu NWS projects 6-10 inches of additional rain on Kauaʻi, with isolated totals up to 16 inches. Oʻahu and Maui County could receive 4-8 inches with isolated totals near 10 inches, while the Big Island could see isolated amounts up to 12 inches. Significant flash flooding, landslides and road closures are possible, especially on Kauaʻi and across southern and eastern portions of the Big Island.

Rapidly building surf will create another serious threat. South-facing shores of Kauaʻi could see waves reach 20-30 feet this afternoon, while damaging surf, coastal flooding and erosion may affect Kauaʻi and possibly Oʻahu as the swell peaks near high tide. Coastal roads and infrastructure could be damaged.

Lowell’s outer rainbands may also produce short-lived tornadoes or waterspouts, primarily around Kauaʻi and Niʻihau Monday into Monday night. Conditions should gradually improve Tuesday as Lowell moves north, but residents should complete preparations immediately and remain alert for rapidly changing warnings‼️🌀

⚠HAWAII UPDATE | SEPT 7 2026 5 AM HST ⚠

Hurricane Lowell's track continues to shift EAST, closer to Hawaii. 

A tropical storm watch has been issued for O'ahu where there is a chance, especially on the western end of the island, to see a brief period of sustained tropical storm winds (40-45 mph) overnight. 

With the track farther east, the western part of Kauai County may also get into sustained hurricane winds around midnight. 

Stronger winds mean a higher chance of wind damage across Kauai, especially overnight when the strongest part of the storm will be moving through. Downed trees, tree branches & powerlines are the biggest concern. Property damage is possible from these downed trees.    

Higher winds also mean more surge. South shore of Kauai may see 2-4' of storm surge overnight & Tuesday morning.

The closer approach of the storm also means more heavy rain. Rainfall forecast has been increased with the heaviest amounts now upward of 16" on Kauai & 10"+ on the Big Island, Maui & O'ahu. Flash flooding & landslides are possible overnight. Travel is not recommended, especially at night.

The worst of the storm will arrive Monday evening local time & last through sunrise Tuesday. Lowell is a fast moving storm so conditions will improve rapidly on Tuesday after sunrise as the eye of the storm gets north of Hawaii & moves away. 

I'll have updates throughout the day on the potential for more track changes. It's certianly possible that Lowell may come even closer to the state.

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
What an incredible view from the Hurricane Hunters as they fly into the eye of major Hurricane Lowell!

That towering wall of white clouds surrounding the clear blue sky is the eyewall, the most vicious and destructive part of a hurricane, where the strongest winds and most intense weather are found. In a powerful hurricane, those thunderstorms can tower more than 50,000 feet into the atmosphere.

You can also see what’s known as the “stadium effect.” The eyewall slopes outward with height, making the view from inside the eye look like you’re standing on the field of a massive stadium with the clouds rising like walls all around you.

The fringe of Lowell is impacting the western islands of Hawaii including Kauai and Oahu with gusty winds and heavy rain today through Tuesday.

We’ve got spoons!!!! ❄️❄️❄️❄️

 Every fall I love seeing some of the old weather folklore start making the rounds, and this one is a classic.

According to folklore, if you cut open a locally grown persimmon seed, the shape inside can supposedly give us a hint about the winter ahead:

🥄 Spoon = lots of snow think “snow shovel”
🔪 Knife = bitter cold and cutting winds
🍴 Fork = a milder winter with lighter snow 

Well… take a look at these seeds. Those sure look like SPOONS to me! 🥄

So if you believe the old folklore, somebody might want to make sure the snow shovel is ready this winter. 

Is it scientific? Nope. Even climate researchers who have looked at the tradition say there isn’t evidence that the shape actually predicts the upcoming winter. 

But weather folklore is part of the fun of watching the seasons change.

What do you see 

spoon, knife or fork?

HAWAII | Sunce late last week, the NHC has updated & tweaked the storm forecast & adjusted some arrival times. 

Earlier it looked like tropical storm wind would reach Kauai County in western Hawaii by Labor Day morning, local time. Now it looks like that won’t happen until later in the afternoon. 

Some things to consider that you can still do through Monday morning:

⚠️Yard & Exterior

 * Clear the lānai: Patio furniture, gas grills, trash bins, umbrellas, and hanging orchid baskets become airborne surprisingly fast in 45-mph gusts. Bring them indoors or into a garage/shed; don't just push them against an exterior wall.

 * Trim heavy foliage and harvest early: Cut dead palm fronds, thin out heavy banana stalks, and harvest heavy fruits (coconuts, breadfruit, papayas) near windows, parked cars, or power drops. High trade or tropical winds snap heavy branches easily.

 * Secure solar panels and loose roofing: Check for loose corrugated metal sheets, flashing, or solar array mounts. At 50 mph, wind can catch the undersides of unanchored panels or loose sheet-metal overhangs.

⚠️Windows & Water Intrusion

 * Crank and latch jalousie (louvered) windows: Common across older island single-wall homes, jalousies leak wind-driven rain heavily. Ensure every louver is fully turned tight, inspect rubber gaskets, and wedge towels along sills to catch water.

 * Brace sliding glass doors: High winds exert significant lateral pressure on large glass tracks. Place a wooden dowel or security bar in the slider channel to prevent the door from rattling or popping off its track.

 * Clear gutters and downspouts: Tropical storms bring intense bursts of rain alongside wind. Clogged roof drains and ʻauwai (drainage ditches) back up quickly, causing overflow into eaves and foundations.

⚠️Island-Specific Infrastructure

 * Catchment system prep: If your property relies on rainwater harvesting, disconnect the downspout diverter before the storm hits. Strong winds blow salt spray, bird droppings, and loose vegetative debris onto the roof, which will contaminate your holding tank if washed in.

 * Prep for localized power cuts: Tree limbs on overhead lines are the primary cause of outages at this wind tier. Charge portable power banks, test flashlights, and verify that solar-battery backup systems or backup generators have fuel and are clear of standing water.

 * Account for local microclimates: Depending on your location relative to the mountains (e.g., Pali corridors, gulches, or downslope leeward areas), local terrain can funnel and accelerate 40-mph regional winds into 60+ mph localized gusts. Take extra care if your property sits in a known wind-venturi channel.

Should really, really read this if you dealt with, or plan to deal with a tropical system in the future.
   This is something 99% of the population isn't aware of when it comes to "sustained wind speeds", and quick "gusts" in hurricanes, and it's probably going to be opposite of what you thought.
    When you see a hurricane with "sustained" winds of 130 mph making landfall, you will be very hard pressed to even find "gusts" that are near those high "sustained, 60 second average" wind speeds found by Hurricane Hunter Aircraft. 
   Those sustained speeds are found over the ocean, well away from land, 30 feet above the ocean, and they search for a while to find that high number. 
   Basically, a good rule of thumb is, the quick "gusts" measured along the beach (on land) will usually only match, or even be a bit less than what the Hurricane Hunter Aircraft finds as a sustained 1 minute average wind speed. Just look up Andrew top gusts, Laura, Delta, Rita, Ike, Ian etc.
   With that being said, when it came to "Tropical Storm" Edouard, many gusts were found in the 70 to 80 mph range.....about what you would find in a category 1 hurricane.

items.text:
The CFS model is already going bullish on a potentially snowy winter across the Southern & Eastern United States...

The newest run depicts a strongly El Niño-like winter pattern, though September climate model forecasts remain highly uncertain and should be taken with a very heavy grain of salt. The model projects below-average snowfall across the Pacific Northwest and Great Lakes, alongside above-average snowfall stretching from the southern Plains into the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast.

Long-range snowfall forecasts this far in advance have very limited skill and cannot reliably anticipate shorter-term winter drivers, including sudden stratospheric warming events and the eventual extent of Eurasian snow cover (especially across Siberia). Additionally, individual model runs can fluctuate significantly from run to run.

That said, this particular pattern is broadly consistent with what we'd expect from a strong El Niño. During strong El Niño events, the subtropical jet typically shifts southward and extends eastward, favoring increased moisture and storm activity across the southern tier of the United States. This storm track historically favors below-average snowfall across portions of the northern United States, particularly the Pacific Northwest and Great Lakes, while increasing precipitation and the potential for significant snowfall farther south and along the East Coast.

One important thing to note: this is a model signal, not a winter forecast. Current guidance strongly favors a very strong El Niño this winter, which does increase confidence in the broad-scale pattern, but the eventual snowfall distribution will depend heavily on shorter-term atmospheric patterns that cannot be predicted with much confidence in early September.

Important Lowell Update: 
   Hurricane Lowell's eye has dilated even more after completing multiple eyewall replacement cycles. The eyewall measures a whopping 70 miles from west to east.
   With subtle, but continuous adjustments east in modeling, along with the ever expanding wind field, it's now possible Kauai could be impacted by near hurricane force gusts, 20 to 30 foot waves, and 12 to 20 inches of rain (especially mountainous areas).
   Even with the system getting kicked in the teeth by shear starting tomorrow, the impacts could be somewhat significant on Kauai given Lowell's increasing wind field/ocean disruption. 
 This will occur Monday night into Tuesday morning.

The first significant snow of the season could arrive in the Northwest and northern U.S. Rockies next weekend! A cold storm system may dig south from western Canada, bringing much cooler weather, lower snow levels and accumulating snow to the highest elevations. Around 70% of ensemble solutions indicate another storm will affect the northern U.S. Rockies, with snow above 7,000 feet along the Continental Divide next Saturday.

Confidence in the exact track, snow levels and amounts remains low this far out. However, anyone planning to travel into the mountains to enjoy the fall colors should monitor the forecast - especially near the higher passes, where an early taste of winter may create slick travel❄️

items.author: MikeCollierWx
items.text:
WINTER LOVERS… this is getting interesting.

It’s only early September, so there is a LONG way to go before winter, but the early signals continue to catch my attention.

Two different seasonal models, the CFSv2 and CanSIPS, are currently showing above normal snowfall across parts of Oklahoma and the central/southern Plains this winter. The CFSv2 signal is particularly impressive, with the above normal snowfall corridor extending from the southern Plains through the Tennessee/Ohio Valley and into the Northeast.

Now, nobody should look at a September seasonal model and start measuring the kids for snow boots. These forecasts will change many times between now and December.

But here’s what has my attention: we continue to see multiple pieces of guidance leaning toward a potentially more active winter across our part of the country.

There’s also a fascinating wrinkle developing with the Pacific pattern. If we end up with a stronger El Niño while the PDO remains negative, we don’t have a nice collection of historical winters that perfectly matches what we’re seeing. That makes simply grabbing an old El Niño winter and calling it an “analog” much less useful.

So no, I’m definitely not forecasting specific snowfall totals in September.

But am I becoming increasingly interested in the possibility of more snow than normal in Oklahoma this winter?

Absolutely.

Winter lovers, you have my attention. 👀

SEVERE STORMS DEVELOPING ACROSS THE SOUTHEAST⚠️💨a Severe Thunderstorm Watch is in effect until 9 PM EDT for western and central South Carolina, western North Carolina and far eastern Georgia.

Strong daytime heating combined with a very humid air mass is creating plenty of instability for thunderstorms to intensify this afternoon. Clusters of storms are expected to move generally south-southeast through the region into this evening. Scattered damaging wind gusts up to 70 mph are the primary threat, with isolated large hail up to around 1 inch also possible. The greatest severe weather risk is focused across parts of Georgia and the Carolinas, although isolated strong to severe storms are also possible farther west into Alabama and the Lower Mississippi Valley.

Remember, a watch means conditions are favorable for severe thunderstorms. Be prepared to move indoors quickly if a warning is issued for your location⚠️💨
